events.article_text:
Iraq Delays Up to 30 Million Barrels of Crude Oil Shipments

What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the…

Crude oil prices were set to book a weekly gain after a string of losses, as increasingly frequent reports about tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz undermined expectations of a glut. Data showing lower than pre-war levels of energy commodity exports from the Middle East also contributed, as did the latest Houthi attacks on Saudi energy targets.

At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $96.61 per barrel, and West Texas Intermediate was changing hands for $85.79 per barrel. Both are still down from heights reached in October but are regaining ground from their latest slump. According to some analysts, if the situation in the Middle East escalates further, Brent could rebound above $100 per barrel.

“We think Brent can still push above USD100/bbl without another major escalation in the Middle East, but that increasingly requires evidence of constrained deliverable supply,” ANZ commodity analysts said this week, as quoted by Reuters.

“Recent attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including areas around the key Ras Tanura export hub and Red Sea ports, alongside reports of vessels being targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, have brought supply risks back into focus,” ING analysts wrote in a note Thursday, noting that traders will also be watching the OPEC+ meeting this weekend to see where the group is heading with its production strategy.

To be fair, supply has been in focus for months now, but in recent weeks, expectations of a glut took over the oil market coverage as the International Energy Agency assumed the September rebound in export rates would hold despite the absence of a peace deal between the United States and Iran, and any sign of willingness for compromise on either side.

Now, data is showing that the IEA’s assumption has been wrong—oil flows are down from September and October highs, and LNG export rates are still half of what they used to be before the war started.

analysis.tldr: Rising oil prices due to Middle East attacks mean India's import costs will likely climb, which can make petrol, diesel, and everyday goods pricier.
the_story: Crude oil prices were heading for a weekly gain because of tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi attacks on Saudi energy targets.
Brent crude traded at $96.61 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate traded at $85.79 per barrel, recovering from a recent slump.
Data showed that energy commodity exports from the Middle East are lower than pre-war levels, proving earlier expectations of an oil glut wrong.
analysis.what_happened: Global oil prices rose because ongoing attacks on shipping lanes and energy targets in the Middle East made traders worry about oil shortages. This fear pushed past earlier predictions that the world had too much oil.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major grocery delivery route getting blocked by protests, causing shop owners to panic and immediately hike food prices because fewer trucks are getting through.
why_it_matters_india: Middle East supply risks and attacks disrupt oil flows -> Global crude oil prices rise.
India imports a large share of its crude oil -> India has to pay more dollars to buy the same amount of oil.
The government and oil companies spend more to buy oil -> The cost of making and transporting everyday goods goes up, pushing up inflation (the rate at which prices rise).
Higher import bills mean India needs more dollars -> The rupee weakens (each rupee buys fewer dollars), making imports even costlier.

impacts.rationale: Attacks on Middle East supply hubs directly push global oil prices higher, which is bad for importing countries like India.
Costlier oil means India needs more dollars to pay for imports, which usually weakens the rupee—making travel and imported goods more expensive for regular people.
Higher crude prices eventually trickle down to transport, manufacturing, and food costs, creating higher inflation that reduces household purchasing power.

watch_next: The upcoming OPEC+ (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, a group of major oil-producing nations) meeting on production strategy
Further updates on security and tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz
analysis.caveats: If oil-producing nations suddenly decide to pump much more oil, prices could drop despite the Middle East tensions.

analysis.tldr: Rising oil prices and a fresh government borrowing plan are making bonds fall, which ultimately pushes up borrowing costs for everyone.
the_story: Indian government bonds decreased in early trading due to rising oil prices and cautious investor sentiment.

The benchmark (standard reference) 6.94% 2036 bond yield (the annual return the government pays investors) increased significantly amid higher expectations for a rate hike (an increase in central bank interest rates).
New Delhi is set to raise 330 billion rupees through a bond sale, contributing to market tension.

Concerns over food-price pressures and inflation (general rise in prices) continue to influence the Reserve Bank of India's [India's central bank that manages money and interest rates] upcoming decision.
analysis.what_happened: Indian government bonds dropped because crude oil prices are rising and the government is preparing to borrow a massive 330 billion rupees through a new debt sale. When the government tries to sell a lot of debt at once, investors demand higher returns (yields), driven by worries that inflation and food prices will force the central bank to raise interest rates.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local grocery shop trying to borrow money from the neighborhood while everyone knows food prices are spiking and the shop owner is already drowning in debt; people will only lend if they are promised much higher interest.
why_it_matters_india: Global crude oil prices stay elevated, fueling domestic inflation concerns.
The government announces a massive 330 billion rupee bond sale, increasing the supply of debt in the market.
Investors demand higher returns to buy these bonds, causing bond yields to jump and bond prices to fall.
Higher benchmark yields ripple through the economy, signaling costlier loans for regular citizens and businesses.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: Higher government borrowing and inflation worries push yields higher, which is generally bad as it raises borrowing costs across the economy.
Elevated oil and food prices feed directly into higher everyday costs for households, which is bad for consumers.

impacts.target: Bank stock prices like SBI, Axis Bank & HDFC Bank
impacts.rationale: Rising bond yields can sometimes hurt the value of bonds that banks already hold, putting temporary pressure on banking shares.

watch_next: The final outcome and investor demand for the 330 billion rupee government bond sale
Upcoming statements from the Reserve Bank of India regarding interest rates and inflation
analysis.caveats: If oil prices drop unexpectedly, inflation fears could ease and bond markets might recover quickly.

analysis.tldr: Record farm output and heavy focus on pulses and oilseeds could help keep everyday food prices stable for households.
the_story: Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan projected Kharif (summer-sown) foodgrain production at 167.14 million tonnes for the 2026-27 crop year.
This target was set despite weather challenges, including El Nino (a weather pattern that usually brings poor rains) and a delayed monsoon (seasonal rains arriving later than normal).
In the previous crop year, overall foodgrain production reached a record high of 378.54 million tonnes.
The government is actively prioritizing pulses (lentils) and oilseeds (crops used to make cooking oil) because India relies heavily on imports for them.
analysis.what_happened: The government announced its official estimate for summer crop production at 167.14 million tonnes. This happened despite bad weather hurdles like El Nino and a delayed monsoon, showing that farming resilience or larger planting areas helped protect the harvest.
analysis.analogy: It is like a gardener managing to grow a record harvest of vegetables despite a surprise drought and a late start to the watering season, keeping the local vegetable market well-stocked.
why_it_matters_india: Good crop production keeps food supplies steady across the country.
Steady supplies prevent sudden spikes in food prices, which helps control overall inflation (the rate at which prices rise).
Lower food inflation means household grocery budgets remain manageable.
Focusing on pulses and oilseeds aims to reduce India's heavy import bills for cooking oils and lentils over time.

impacts.rationale: Strong foodgrain production keeps food supplies high, which generally lowers inflation—good news for household budgets.
Government prioritization and steady output can cool down everyday kitchen staple prices, making things cheaper for consumers.

watch_next: Actual weather conditions and final rainfall distribution during the monsoon season
Updates on government procurement and buffer stock levels for foodgrains
analysis.caveats: The text is very brief and based on early projections, so actual final harvest numbers could change depending on future weather shifts.

events.headline: Trade-facilitating measures help offset rise in new G20 trade restrictions

items.title: Trade-facilitating measures help offset rise in new G20 trade restrictions
items.summary: The number of tariff increases and other non-facilitating trade measures introduced by G20 economies rose sharply in the first half of 2026, and the stockpile of such measures reached a record level, according to the WTO's latest report on G20 trade measures. At the same time, G20 economies, representing around 80-85 per cent of global GDP and 75 per cent of international trade, introduced a significant number of trade-facilitating measures, helping to reinforce global trade flows despite heightened geopolitical tensions and economic uncertainty.

events.article_text:
trade monitoring — Joint reports on G-20 trade and investment measures

Stockpile of other-import and other-export measures in force since 2009

In 2025, G20 economies introduced 874 new trade and trade-related measures and a further 697 during the first half of 2026 alone. This includes a range of new measures as well as adjustments to existing trade measures, including changes to tariffs, export controls, and sector-specific measures as G20 economies navigate a complex global environment. The increase in trade policy activity was broad-based and not limited to the G20 economies, as noted by the WTO-wide monitoring report published on 29 October 2026, which can be accessed here.

G20 economies introduced 206 new restrictive and other non-facilitating trade measures in the first half of 2026, compared to 194 recorded during all of 2025. Import-related measures amounted to USD 2.0 trillion (12.9 per cent of G20 imports) in the first half of 2026, compared with USD 2.8 trillion (19.1 per cent) in all of 2025. These are the two highest levels on record and around ten times higher than those recorded over the past 15 years. Export-related measures, including changes in tariffs and export controls, soared to 4.8 per cent of G20 exports (USD 711 billion), compared to 0.9 per cent in 2025 (representing USD 126 billion), marking the highest level on record.

At the same time, new trade-facilitating measures accelerated sharply in the first half of 2026. G20 economies introduced 282 such measures, exceeding the 225 recorded during all of 2025. These import-facilitating measures covered an estimated USD 977 billion (6.4 per cent of G20 imports), compared with USD 1.1 trillion (7.8 per cent) in 2025. Export-facilitating measures reached USD 560 billion (3.8 per cent of G20 exports), more than five times the USD 101 billion (0.7 per cent) recorded in 2025, marking the highest level on record. Much of this increase reflected temporary responses to trade disruptions associated with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, including tariff reductions and removals.

The report covers trade and trade-related measures up to 30 June 2026, presenting annual data for 2025 and semi-annual data for 2026. It also tracks the value of trade covered by measures introduced since 2009, known as "the stockpile," that remained in force as of the reporting date.

As of 30 June 2026, the stockpile of import-related restrictive and other non-facilitating measures introduced since 2009 reached USD 4.5 trillion, impacting 29.6 per cent of G20 imports, a rise from 27.9 per cent at the end of 2025. The stockpile of export-related measures also reached USD 1.3 trillion, covering 9.1 per cent of G20 exports, up from 5.4 per cent at the end of 2025.

WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala said: "On the one hand, we are witnessing that import tariffs and other non-facilitating measures are significantly impacting global trade, with the stockpile of trade-restrictive and other non-facilitating measures reaching its highest level since WTO trade monitoring began in 2009. As of 30 June 2026, more than four-fifths of these measures affecting imports and exports were introduced by G20 economies, underscoring their substantial influence on global trade flows. On the other hand, G20 economies have demonstrated a commendable effort in keeping trade flowing-accounting for nearly three-quarters of all imports benefiting from WTO trade-facilitating actions and almost all exports benefiting from export-facilitating measures during 2025 and the first half of 2026.

She added: "I welcome these trade-facilitating efforts and urge WTO members to leverage this positive momentum, while exercising restraint in introducing new trade restrictions. Committing to fostering open, predictable, and transparent trade practices is essential for stimulating economic growth and preserving the valuable benefits of the multilateral trading system."

Global trade proved more resilient than projected in the first half of 2026, despite ongoing disruptions from the Middle East conflict, driven largely by surging demand for AI-enabling goods. On 8 October, the WTO revised its forecast for world merchandise trade volume growth in 2026 upward to 3.9 per cent, more than double the previous baseline forecast of 1.9 per cent issued in March. In value terms, merchandise trade increased by around 15 per cent year-on-year during the first half of 2026.

On the other hand, commercial services trade growth is now forecast at 3.3 per cent in 2026, reflecting a decrease from the March forecast of 4.8 per cent largely due to the impact of the Middle East conflict on transport and travel services. Nevertheless, in value terms, commercial services trade increased by around 14 per cent in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025.

Trade remedy actions continued to be widely utilized across G20 economies, although the trade affected by these measures remained limited. In 2025, G20 economies initiated 455 trade remedy actions, comprising 345 initiations and 110 terminations, with initiations averaging 28.8 per month. During the first half of 2026, 209 new trade remedy actions were recorded, including 188 initiations and 21 terminations, with the monthly average of new initiations rising to 31.3. Anti-dumping measures remained the most frequently utilized trade remedy instrument.

G20 economies continued to utilize the transparency mechanisms of the Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) and Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT) Committees at the WTO to notify their related measures and to constructively address specific trade concerns without resorting to dispute settlement.

The report emphasizes the ongoing dialogue among G20 economies devoted to addressing underlying trade imbalances, coupled with intensified efforts to reach negotiated solutions.

G20 economies remained key players in global trade, while continuing to navigate the ongoing challenges posed by geopolitical t

analysis.tldr: A surge in global trade restrictions by major economies could make imported goods costlier for Indians, but easing measures in some areas also helps keep supply chains moving.
the_story: In the first half of 2026, G20 economies (a group of the world's major economies) introduced 206 new trade-restrictive measures, surpassing the 194 recorded during all of 2025.
Import-related restrictions hit record highs, touching USD 2.0 trillion in the first half of 2026, while export restrictions soared to USD 711 billion (4.8% of G20 exports).

At the same time, governments rushed to introduce trade-facilitating measures—like tariff reductions and removals—reaching 282 actions in early 2026, partly as temporary responses to trade disruptions from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala noted that while restrictive measures are at their highest level since monitoring began in 2009, G20 economies also led efforts to keep trade flowing through facilitation.
Despite Middle East conflicts impacting transport services, global merchandise trade grew around 15% year-on-year in early 2026, driven heavily by demand for AI-enabling goods.
analysis.what_happened: Major world economies introduced a record number of new trade barriers and restrictions like tariffs and export controls in early 2026. However, they simultaneously rolled out a large wave of trade-easing measures—such as temporary tariff cuts—to offset disruptions caused by events like the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
analysis.analogy: It is like a highway authority putting up more toll booths and speed limits (trade restrictions), but at the same time opening up special fast-lanes and lowering fees on other routes (trade-facilitating measures) to prevent total traffic jams.
why_it_matters_india: Major global economies add trade barriers and tariffs -> Global supply chains face friction and higher costs -> Import prices for raw materials and goods can rise globally -> Consumer prices in India face upward pressure.

Governments introduce trade-facilitating measures and tariff cuts to counter disruptions -> Certain shipping routes and goods face lower hurdles -> Indian exporters trading with these regions may find temporary relief.
Global demand shifts toward AI and tech-enabling goods -> World merchandise trade grows despite regional conflicts -> Indian technology and engineering sectors see shifting export demand patterns.

Geopolitical tensions and trade restrictions pile up into a massive multi-trillion-dollar stockpile -> Global trade becomes less predictable -> Foreign investors may reassess risk, affecting capital flows into emerging markets like India.

impacts.target: Imported electronic and industrial goods prices in India
impacts.rationale: Record-high global import restrictions and tariffs make buying foreign components costlier, which is generally bad for Indian consumers and manufacturing businesses relying on imported inputs.
While global trade restrictions create friction, resilient world trade growth and surging demand for tech goods provide some support for export-oriented Indian companies.

impacts.target: Global crude oil and transport-related shipping costs
impacts.rationale: Middle East conflicts and transit disruptions like the Strait of Hormuz push up shipping and energy costs, leading to costlier fuel imports for India—which is bad for household budgets.

watch_next: Future updates from the WTO on whether G20 nations add more restrictions or keep easing them
Developments regarding trade disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and Middle East conflict zones
Shifts in global tech and AI-enabling goods demand that drive merchandise trade growth
analysis.caveats: The report reflects historical data up to June 2026, and sudden geopolitical escalations could rapidly shift countries toward even harsher protectionism.

events.headline: Underused land can support fodder production [Commentary]

items.title: Underused land can support fodder production [Commentary]
items.summary: In March 2024, the fields around Baramati in Maharashtra’s Pune district began to tell a familiar story of a semi-arid region. The maize and sorghum grown for fodder after the monsoon were largely exhausted, summer fields remained dry, and livestock farmers increasingly depended on crop residues, sugarcane tops and purchased feed. During our (ICAR-NIASM) survey of […]

events.article_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

In March 2024, the fields around Baramati in Maharashtra’s Pune district began to tell a familiar story of a semi-arid region. The maize and sorghum grown for fodder after the monsoon were largely exhausted, summer fields remained dry, and livestock farmers increasingly depended on crop residues, sugarcane tops and purchased feed. During our (ICAR-NIASM) survey of 60 livestock-keeping families in the rainfed Baramati, farmers reported seasonal shifts in fodder sources. Maize silage accounted for about 90% of dry fodder during kharif and about 88% during rabi, while sorghum accounted for about 93% during summer. Nearly 96% of farmers identified lack of quality fodder as a major problem, while around 87% reported fodder scarcity during drought.

What farmers experience in Baramati reflects a much larger national challenge of fodder scarcity in arid regions. Maharashtra faces an estimated deficit of 31.3% in dry fodder and 59.4% in green fodder, while fodder crops occupy only about 3% of its cultivated area, according to 2020 estimates by ICAR-Indian Grassland and Fodder Research Institute, Jhansi.

In rainfed regions such as Pune district, where limited water makes year-round fodder production difficult, fodder scarcity is therefore not simply an animal-feed problem — it is a livelihood and climate-resilience challenge.

The question is no longer simply how to produce more fodder, but how to ensure reliable, nutritious feed when water is scarce and climate variability is increasing. Perennial, water-efficient fodder systems can offer a practical pathway towards year-round fodder availability while strengthening livestock-based livelihoods in drought-prone landscapes.

We, a group of scientists from ICAR-NIASM, thought about how farmers can produce more fodder without sacrificing food and cash crops production. This led us to explore whether degraded patches, fallow land and field boundaries could become reliable fodder sources. The result was the climate-resilient CHARA Bank, developed by Indian Council of Agricultural Research-National Institute of Abiotic Stress Management (ICAR-NIASM) with support from NABARD, Pune. The concept is to use about 1,000 sq m (one-fourth of an acre) of underutilised land to establish a perennial fodder reserve that can be harvested repeatedly through the year.

Unlike seasonal maize or sorghum, CHARA Bank combines perennial fodder trees, grasses and legumes that provide repeated harvests for several years. Deep-rooted species access deeper soil moisture, while nitrogen-fixing legumes improve soil fertility, ensuring a more reliable fodder supply with less frequent replanting.

Farms vary in their soil conditions, irrigation access and available space, so a single design may not work everywhere. A farmer with irrigated black soil has different options from one cultivating shallow murrum soil, while those with limited spare land may be able to make use of existing field bunds.

To accommodate these differences, we developed three CHARA Bank models: a multi-tier model (boundary), a silvipasture model and a boundary plantation model for the field edges and bunds. Long-term field trials were conducted to evaluate perennial fodder and silvipasture combinations on degraded soils. Different tree densities and cutting heights of grasses and legumes were tested, and promising combinations were validated in farmers’ fields to develop suitable CHARA Bank models.

This experience helped shape the CHARA Bank project with NABARD. Fodder does not always need prime agricultural land. By treating degraded patches, fallow areas and field boundaries as productive assets, farmers can create a small, perennial “fodder bank” that supports livestock while conserving their best land for food and cash crops.

On 21 farmers’ fields, the systems produced about 9-22 tonnes of green fodder annually from just 1,000 sq m, showing how small areas can become productive fodder resources.

The fodder was also nutritionally valuable. Laboratory analysis showed crude protein ranging from 9.3% in Cenchrus grass to 28.2% in Sesbania, while Desmanthus and Leucaena contained about 23.6% and 23.5%, respectively.

During our 2024 survey and discussions with farmers, we found that dairy animals were commonly receiving 8-11 kg of concentrate a day, costing about ₹240-400 and accounting for roughly 40–50% of rearing costs. The aim was therefore not to replace the entire ration with green fodder, but to use protein-rich fodder to reduce dependence on costly concentrates.

The results were encouraging. In a 90-day trial with Holstein-Friesian cows, feeding 5 kg of CHARA Bank green fodder per animal per day reduced concentrate use from 9 to 6 kg/day — a 33% reduction. Milk yield remained stable to slightly higher, rising from 17.05 to 17.69 litres/day, while milk fat increased from 4.36% to 4.75%. At local prices, this represented an estimated additional return ranging from ₹2,670 to ₹26,000 per cow per lactation.

A similar response was observed in Murrah buffaloes. Feeding 3-4 kg of green fodder reduced concentrate use by about 29%, while milk yield increased by 17.5%. Estimated additional returns ranged from ₹6,830 to ₹38,000 per buffalo per lactation, depending on animal and lactation performance.

We also tested the model with goats. Young Osmanabadi goats fed fodder from the multi-tier and silvipasture systems for seven months showed about 94% higher weight gain than goats under conventional farmer feeding, along with improvements in haemoglobin and other blood-health indicators. The additional return was estimated at about ₹2,600 per goat. A 10-guntha (1000 square metres) fodder bank could support a small unit of about seven goats — six females and one male — through the year.

analysis.tldr: New low-cost fodder farming models can lower daily expenses for dairy and livestock farmers, potentially boosting milk and meat production profits.
the_story: A March 2024 survey of 60 livestock-keeping families in Baramati, Maharashtra, revealed that 96% face major quality fodder shortages, and 87% suffer shortages during droughts.

Scientists from ICAR-NIASM, supported by NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development), developed the 'CHARA Bank' using 1,000 square meters of underutilized or degraded land for perennial fodder reserves.
Field trials on 21 farms produced 9 to 22 tonnes of green fodder annually from that small space, helping farmers reduce expensive commercial feed concentrates by nearly a third.

Trials on Holstein-Friesian cows, Murrah buffaloes, and Osmanabadi goats showed stable or higher milk yields, improved milk fat, and higher weight gains, adding thousands of rupees in extra returns per animal.
analysis.what_happened: Scientists and agricultural researchers designed a new land-use system called the CHARA Bank to tackle severe animal feed shortages in dry regions like Maharashtra. By growing resilient trees, grasses, and legumes on unused patches and field boundaries instead of prime crop land, farmers can harvest nutritious feed year-round.
analysis.analogy: It is like planting a small, self-renewing vegetable patch on your apartment's balcony so you stop having to buy expensive pre-packaged meals from the grocery store every single day.
why_it_matters_india: Improved livestock feed availability reduces daily rearing costs for rural dairy and goat farmers.
Lower input costs and higher milk/meat production increase overall household earnings for rural livestock owners.
Reduced reliance on commercial feed concentrates eases household cash-flow pressures in rural farming communities.
Better-fed livestock improve productivity in India's broader rural dairy and agricultural economy.

impacts.target: Rural household incomes for dairy and livestock farmers
impacts.rationale: lower feeding costs and higher milk/meat yields mean more money in farmers' pockets — good for rural consumers.

impacts.target: Commercial feed (concentrate) demand in rural areas
impacts.rationale: farmers can replace expensive store-bought feed with homegrown fodder — good for livestock owners saving money.
this is a localized agricultural development with minimal direct impact on large publicly traded companies.

watch_next: Adoption rates of CHARA Bank models by farmers outside Maharashtra
Support and funding announcements from NABARD or state agricultural departments
analysis.caveats: The success of these fodder banks depends heavily on local soil types, water availability, and whether individual farmers adopt the multi-tier planting models.

events.headline: Mint Quick Edit | Trump's tariff tantrum should prompt clarity and calm from New Delhi

items.title: Mint Quick Edit | Trump's tariff tantrum should prompt clarity and calm from New Delhi
items.summary: US President Donald Trump's latest threat to levy tariffs of upto 25% on Indian goods may be a pressure tactic amid negotiations for an India-US trade deal. New Delhi mustn't get rattled. Here's what policymakers should consider.

events.article_text:
Despite the mid-term election losses suffered by the Republican Party, US President Donald Trump is in no mood to give up on tariff threats as an instrument of state policy. The Trump administration has now proposed a fresh slew of tariffs on trade partners.

Indian imports could face a new tariff rate of up to 25%. The US trade representative has said the tariff rate could be brought down to 17% if the Indo-US trade deal goes through. India and the US had earlier agreed on a framework for an interim deal with an 18% tariff rate.

The latest tariff threat could be a pressure tactic to get New Delhi to sign on the dotted line, and bring an end to the long-pending Indo-US trade deal. Delhi must stay calm and continue to deepen trade relationships with a diverse set of trade partners even while it continues trade talks with the US.

Delhi should also ensure that Indian business do not face trade-related troubles at home. At a time when Indian exporters are already facing an uncertain global environment, policymakers should make a concerted effort to ease their troubles by lowering import duties and rationalizing customs rules and classifications.

The Mint Editorial Board is a panel of editorial writers with expertise across diverse domains of relevance to the newspaper’s opinion readers. The Board draws on long years of experience in business, financial and economic journalism, apart from other professional fields, although each member’s record of coverage, analysis and commentary would reveal far broader interests. This panel keeps itself in tune with the news as it unfolds and aims to reflect Mint’s views, but cannot claim a daily consensus on every issue of debate that matters. As a matter of routine, the Mint Editorial Board produces the newspaper’s Quick Edit, a snappy daily comment on pressing issues, and Our View, a full-length editorial on an issue that demands urgent attention. These are often matters of policy but cover a lot more, as readers may attest. The Board’s mission in expressing opinions, done in the spirit of a "nation in conversation with itself", is aligned with that of Mint: to be "an unbiased and clear-minded chronicler of the Indian Dream".

analysis.tldr: New US tariff threats could make it harder for Indian businesses to sell goods to America, requiring India to diversify its trade partners and ease local rules.
the_story: US President Donald Trump has proposed a fresh round of tariffs (taxes on imported goods) on trade partners, despite his party's mid-term election losses.
Indian imports into the US could face a new tariff rate of up to 25%, though the US trade representative says it could drop to 17% if an Indo-US trade deal is completed.
India and the US had previously agreed on a framework for an interim trade deal featuring an 18% tariff rate.
The editorial suggests this tariff threat is a pressure tactic by the US to force India into signing the long-pending trade agreement.
The Mint Editorial Board advises New Delhi to stay calm, continue trade talks with the US while deepening relationships with other countries, and lower domestic import duties to help local exporters.
analysis.what_happened: The US administration has proposed new tariffs of up to 25% on Indian imports, likely as a pressure tactic to force India to finalize a long-pending trade deal. In response, the Mint Editorial Board advises New Delhi to remain calm, keep talking to the US, and simultaneously build trade ties with other countries while easing domestic rules for Indian businesses.
analysis.analogy: It is like a demanding shopkeeper threatening to raise prices on your regular supplies unless you sign a strict contract today, forcing you to look at other shops while you negotiate.
why_it_matters_india: US proposes up to 25% tariffs on Indian goods -> Indian exporters face higher costs and uncertainty when selling to the US.
Pressure increases on New Delhi -> India must decide whether to sign the trade deal or face steep US import taxes.
Exporters face an uncertain global environment -> The editorial suggests Indian policymakers should lower import duties and simplify customs rules at home to support local businesses.
India diversifies its trade partners -> Spreads out business risk so India is not overly dependent on a single country like the US.

impacts.target: Indian export businesses and manufacturing sectors
impacts.rationale: Higher US tariffs (up to 25%) could squeeze profit margins for Indian companies selling goods to America, which is tough for local businesses.
Uncertainty around global trade rules and pressure on Indian exporters can cause cautious sentiment among investors in the stock market.

watch_next: Whether India and the US formally sign the interim trade deal at the 17% or 18% tariff rate
Any announcement by Indian policymakers to lower import duties or simplify customs rules for local exporters
Progress on India's trade agreements with countries other than the US
analysis.caveats: This opinion piece is based on editorial commentary rather than a finalized government policy announcement from Washington or New Delhi.

analysis.tldr: When the Reserve Bank of India spends fewer dollars to protect our currency, it signals that foreign investments are flowing in to steady the rupee.
the_story: In November, the Reserve Bank of India (India's central bank) significantly reduced its dollar sales.
This decrease in dollar sales was aimed at stabilizing the rupee (our national currency).
A surge in foreign investments into Indian equities (shares of companies) helped push up the rupee's value, allowing it to recover from past lows.
The balance of payments deficit (the gap between money flowing into and out of India) has declined despite some net dollar sales.
analysis.what_happened: The Reserve Bank of India cut back on selling US dollars from its reserves in November. This happened because a wave of foreign money rushed into Indian stock markets, which naturally strengthened the rupee without the central bank needing to step in as much.
analysis.analogy: It is like a parent stopping heavy spending from their emergency savings to support a child's allowance, because the child just started earning their own pocket money from a part-time job.
why_it_matters_india: Foreign investors pour money into Indian shares -> Demand for Indian rupees rises
Stronger demand -> The rupee gains value against the US dollar
RBI steps back -> Central bank needs to sell fewer dollars from its reserves to protect the currency
Overall financial stability improves -> Reduces the balance of payments deficit

impacts.rationale: A stronger rupee makes imported items like crude oil cheaper for India, which is generally good for controlling inflation.
Surging foreign investments in equities boost overall stock market sentiment, which benefits regular investors.

watch_next: Whether foreign investors continue pumping money into Indian stocks
The monthly updates on India's foreign exchange reserves
analysis.caveats: If global markets suddenly turn volatile and foreign investors pull their money back out, the RBI may have to resume heavy dollar sales.

analysis.tldr: Upcoming decisions from India's central bank and rising global oil prices mean borrowing costs might become more unpredictable for everyone.
the_story: Government bond yields [the interest rate the government pays to borrow] have stayed in a narrow, stable range this week due to conflicting data.

Traders are being cautious and waiting for the Reserve Bank of India [India's central bank that controls money and interest rates] monetary policy decision because they expect a rate hike [an increase in benchmark interest rates].
Crude oil [raw petroleum] prices have recently gone up, which raises worries about India's import bill [total money spent buying goods from abroad] and inflation [rising prices for everyday goods].

The NSE [National Stock Exchange, a major Indian stock market] got approval from the Reserve Bank of India to launch futures contracts [agreements to buy or sell something at a future date at a set price] linked to corporate bond indices [trackers of company debt performance], following earlier Sebi [Securities and Exchange Board of India, the stock market regulator] clearance.
analysis.what_happened: Government bond yields are holding steady while traders wait for the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy update. People expect the central bank to raise interest rates, and global crude oil prices have also ticked up, creating a cautious mood in the markets.
analysis.analogy: It is like waiting outside a store for the manager to announce if prices are going up today, while you watch the cost of fuel for your delivery truck get more expensive.
why_it_matters_india: Crude oil prices go up -> India's import bill increases because we buy most of our oil from abroad
Higher import costs -> Inflation pressures grow, making everyday items pricier for households
Reserve Bank of India considers a rate hike -> Bond yields could get pushed higher
New corporate bond futures get approved -> Investors get tools to manage debt risks and trade more transparently on the market

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: An anticipated rate hike by the central bank could push yields higher, which generally means borrowing costs get more expensive for everyone — bad for borrowers.
Recent increases in crude oil prices can translate to costlier fuel at the pump — bad for household budgets.
Higher import bills from pricier crude oil push up overall costs for goods and services — bad for everyday consumers.

impacts.target: Banking stocks like SBI, Axis Bank, and HDFC Bank
impacts.rationale: Mentioned as trending stocks, their prices fluctuate based on how markets react to upcoming interest rate announcements.

watch_next: The upcoming monetary policy announcement from the Reserve Bank of India
Further movements in global crude oil prices
The launch and rollout of NSE's new corporate bond futures contracts
analysis.caveats: If the central bank surprises markets by keeping rates unchanged instead of hiking them, bond yields could drop.

analysis.tldr: Efforts by China to reduce its reliance on the US dollar could eventually alter global trade payments and currency values, touching the cost of imports and savings for Indian investors.
the_story: Panelists at a Council on Foreign Relations event examined China's efforts to reduce its dependence on the US dollar.
Experts discussed the internationalization of the renminbi (China's official currency), which means expanding its use across borders.
The discussion covered the development of alternative payment systems and China's growing financial ties with emerging markets.
analysis.what_happened: Experts met to discuss how China is trying to build alternatives to the US-dominated financial system. This includes pushing its own currency for global trade and creating new payment networks, driven by a desire to lessen its vulnerability to US financial power.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group of shopkeepers trying to set up a local credit system so they do not have to rely on the town's biggest bank for every single transaction.
why_it_matters_india: China tries to promote its currency (the renminbi) and build alternative payment networks ->
More countries use non-dollar systems for international trade over time ->
Global demand for the US dollar shifts, which can create swings in currency exchange rates globally ->
The rupee (India's currency) and imported goods like oil face indirect pressure from changing global currency dynamics.

impacts.rationale: If global currency systems shift away from the dollar, overall currency market volatility could weaken the rupee, making imports like electronics and crude oil costlier for regular people — generally bad.
Uncertainty around global financial power and the US dollar usually pushes central banks and investors toward safe-haven assets like gold, raising local prices — a mixed impact for buyers.

watch_next: Any major trade deals signed between emerging markets and China settling payments in non-dollar currencies
Updates on the adoption rate of China's cross-border payment systems
analysis.caveats: The article text is a brief event description rather than a reported news story with concrete data, so these impacts reflect long-term hypothetical risks rather than immediate shifts.

history.title: When a real revolution was still a terrible investment
history.what: The Nasdaq fell 78% over two and a half years. Companies that had listed with no profits and enormous valuations went to zero in their hundreds. The internet, meanwhile, continued to transform the world exactly as promised.
history.why: The story was true and the price was wrong — which is the hardest lesson in investing. Capital flooded in because the technology was genuinely revolutionary, so valuations stopped referring to earnings at all and began referring to page views and "eyeballs". Cheap money after the 1998 crisis supplied the fuel; investment bank research supplied the justification.
history.impact: About $5 trillion of market value vanished. It took the Nasdaq fifteen years to regain its 2000 peak. Yet Amazon, which fell 94%, went on to become one of the most valuable companies on earth. Both facts are true at once.
history.policy: Sarbanes-Oxley in 2002 forced chief executives to personally certify their accounts and made auditors independent of consulting arms. Rules were introduced to separate investment bank research from the deal-making desks that had been quietly paying for it.
history.consequence: Corporate accounts became more trustworthy and the cost of going public rose sharply — which is part of why companies now stay private for far longer and list only when they are already large. The Fed also cut rates hard to cushion the bust, which fed the housing boom that broke in 2008.
history.pattern: A transformative technology and a good investment are different questions. The revolution can be entirely real while the shares are still priced for a future that arrives ten years late. Ask what you are paying for the growth, not whether the growth is coming.
history.india_echo: India had its own version. The Sensex IT index collapsed with the Nasdaq and Indian software stocks lost 80%. But Infosys and TCS were real businesses with real dollar earnings, and they compounded for the next twenty years. Today's Indian AI and new-age tech listings are the same question in new clothes.
history.watch_for: Valuation measures being replaced by engagement measures. When you are shown users instead of profits, someone has decided profits are inconvenient.
